reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Shields' Textbook of Glaucoma
clinicalPearls: A secondary angle-closure glaucoma caused by a large, swollen (intumescent) cataractous lens that pushes the iris forward and closes the drainage angle
It typically presents like acute angle closure, with a painful red eye, corneal oedema, a mid-dilated pupil, high pressure, and a shallow anterior chamber
A key clue is an advanced, often mature or intumescent, cataract in the affected eye, frequently with a deeper chamber and open angle in the fellow eye
The swollen lens both increases pupillary block and physically shallows the peripheral angle, so mechanisms overlap
Asymmetry of anterior chamber depth and lens thickness between the two eyes helps distinguish it from primary angle closure, where both eyes tend to be anatomically similar
Initial management lowers pressure medically with topical agents and systemic acetazolamide and controls inflammation, sometimes with laser peripheral iridotomy as a temporising measure
Definitive treatment is removal of the offending lens by cataract surgery once the eye is quietened and pressure reduced
Prolonged high pressure risks optic-nerve damage and permanent synechial closure, so timely lens extraction is important
reference.pathophysiology: Phacomorphic glaucoma occurs when a cataractous lens becomes enlarged and intumescent, swelling with fluid so that it thickens and shifts the iris-lens diaphragm forward. This exaggerates relative pupillary block by increasing lens-iris contact and simultaneously crowds the peripheral angle as the bulky lens pushes the peripheral iris against the trabecular meshwork. Aqueous outflow is obstructed and intraocular pressure rises acutely, producing corneal oedema, pain, and, if sustained, peripheral anterior synechiae and optic-nerve damage. The disparity in lens size and chamber depth compared with the fellow eye reflects the lens as the primary driver, distinguishing it from primary angle closure where both eyes share a predisposing anatomy.
additionalDifferentials: Phacolytic glaucoma from a leaking hypermature cataract
Uveitic glaucoma with a red painful eye
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination documenting an intumescent or mature cataract and shallow chamber
Gonioscopy of both eyes to confirm angle closure and assess the fellow eye
Comparison of anterior chamber depth and lens thickness between eyes, with biometry where possible
Applanation tonometry to quantify the pressure rise
B-scan ultrasonography when the fundus is not visible to exclude posterior pathology
Optic disc assessment for glaucomatous damage once the media clear
redFlags: Acute painful red eye with very high pressure and corneal oedema needing emergency pressure reduction
A mature or intumescent unilateral cataract with unilateral angle closure
Prolonged pressure elevation threatening irreversible optic-nerve damage
Marked asymmetry of chamber depth signalling a lens-driven mechanism
reference.prognosis: Prompt pressure control followed by cataract extraction usually resolves the angle closure and restores vision, but delayed treatment can leave permanent optic-nerve damage, synechial angle closure, and corneal decompensation, and the acutely inflamed eye carries higher surgical risk.
pitfalls: Treating it as primary angle closure and delaying the definitive lens extraction
Overlooking the diagnosis by not comparing the two eyes for asymmetry
Confusing it with phacolytic glaucoma, which involves lens protein leakage rather than pure angle crowding
Assuming iridotomy alone will resolve pressure when the swollen lens must be removed
Operating on a highly inflamed, high-pressure eye without first medically stabilising it
management: Definitive treatment by cataract extraction to remove the intumescent lens and relieve the angle closure
Initial medical pressure control with topical aqueous suppressants and systemic acetazolamide and hyperosmotic agents
Topical corticosteroids and pupil management to reduce inflammation and the pupillary-block component
Laser peripheral iridotomy as a temporising measure to relieve pupillary block before surgery
Corneal clearing and optimisation before surgery, with intraocular lens implantation once pressure and inflammation are controlled
Postoperative monitoring of intraocular pressure, the drainage angle for peripheral anterior synechiae, and the optic nerve
Ophthalmic surgical referral with assessment of the fellow eye angle and lens
